snippet.title: Chiisana Oukoku Eltoria [小さな王国エルトリア] Game Sample - Playstation
snippet.description:
As a low-budget passion project made by a small segment of KSS' staff as a side work in 2000, PS' "Chiiisana Oukoku Eltoria" (also known as "Little Kingdom Eltoria") is a cult-classic hybrid game among Japanese gamers. Retailing at 4,800 yen and with a team of about a dozen people, the game is a unique combination of simulated building and resource management, romantic SLG adventure and RPG. It is most notable for its character designs by Toru Kawaguchi, who also worked on graphic designs for "Tour Party: Sotsugyou Ryokou ni Ikou" and as an animation producer for "Shinreigari" (aka "Ghost Hound", which in turn was scripted by Chiaki J. Konaka of "Serial Experiments Lain" fame and originally designed by Masamune Shirow in 1987). It was re-released for the Japanese PSN as a downloadable title. Here's a rundown for English-speakers.

The general premise of the game is pretty straightforward: The player assumes the role of the unnamed prince of Eltoria, a developing land he is training to inherit from his father. With your royal advisor and mage protector, Elfried, as well as guard siblings (Leon and Erica) and the bumbling but cheerful maid, Daisy, they round out your main entourage as you aim to raise your kingdom to greatness over a period of two years which will determine if you're ready to succeed your father. However, this is only the "surface level" objective, as you will meet many other characters on your quest including the sweet daughter of the local Inn, Flora, a powerful and eccentric witch named Clover, a powerful swordswoman named Sakura, a fortune teller necessary to see the game's true endings named Marigold, a prospective princess love interest named Scarlet, and a variety of other characters as you expand your kingdom's reach and influence.

You see, in the span of two years, you also need to gather information, partake in a variety of time-sensitive events, cultivate your land with a variety of facilities and emerging technologies and even go on a journey to defeat a dragon and topple a demon king. You will also come across a variety of young women on your quest, a few of which are marriage material, and you get the satisfaction of exploring your city and watching it gradually grow into a hub that people all over will visit and one that you can be proud of. While there is not really a day / night cycle, there is an in-game time-tracking system where certain characters and events can only be triggered on certain days. All of this is handled with a relatively simple to understand interface that, for the most part, works as intended, though there are still some obtuse things the game does here and there.

For starters, the game should've had an actual calendar to keep track of important events or days; as an example, Scarlet will often visit on the tenth of every month, "Thanksgiving" (in Eltoria) takes place on October 14th, you collect income from the residents on the 28th of each month, so on and so forth. However, you can miss these events (including the money-making one) which can greatly influence how your run will go. While you can influence the amount of time you spend during planning and expansion, other things have a static time frame such as traveling outside the kingdom or building certain facilities. You also have the option of traveling through your kingdom once a week to converse with NPCs, important characters, shop, trigger events, and more, but you get to choose which day you go (and you need to manually count these out to make sure they don't fall on an important date). It's not too common to miss an important deadline, but it's common enough to require tracking your dates to maximize your run. You'll spend a lot of time plowing fields, building new facilities and chatting it up with others, but you can also tax your people, sell items you find for additional income, and monitor your overall progress and approval rating.

Once you understand the concept, the game runs pretty smoothly, but it's still a modest challenge -- it's very easy to completely ruin a run by doing simple things such as taxing your people too much (which will cause them to revolt if it's over 100% resulting in a Game Over or lower your approval rating too much if it's more than 50%) or not identifying a lucrative income model early on. There are also some very specific quests that require weeks and months of planning and will lock you out of the best endings otherwise (in conjunction with an 85%+ Approval and 90%+ Development Score). Combat is also extremely simple and half-baked with a simple ATB system (characters grow stronger over time, no leveling or real skills, occasional item drops) and the game is very lacking in the audio / visual department (the game has no real spoken dialogue or FMVs and it could easily be reproduced on the SNES / Gen with some minor concessions) but is still unique and charming enough to warrant owning as-is for fans of sims.

This is a video of the game in action. Enjoy.
